newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan agrees port practices need to be reformed.
newsitem.headline: Japan agrees port practices need to be reformed.

text.p: Transport Minister Makoto Koga said on Friday it would be tough to meet U.S. demands for reform of Japan's controversial port practices, but acknowledged that improvements were needed.
Japanese media, meanwhile, agreed Washington had just cause for complaint and lambasted their own government for failing to move more quickly to solve the sticky problem.

The U.S. Federal Maritime Commission (FMC) said on Wednesday it would slap $100,000 surcharges on Japanese vessels calling at U.S. ports in retaliation for what it called "unfavourable restrictive practices". The surcharges would go into effect on April 14.

The FMC says the Japan Harbour Transportation Association (JHTA), which mediates between labour unions and shipping companies, has put in place costly and restrictive practices that discriminate against foreign vessels.
The commission said the JHTA exercises its control through a "prior consultation" system of negotiations and pre-approvals involving carriers, the JHTA and waterfront unions.
Koga, whose ministry on Thursday urged Washington to withdraw the sanctions threat, said it was hard for the government to intervene in matters involving labour unions.
But he added: "I think we should make the system more transparent, as U.S. and Japanese shipping firms are calling for more transparency."

The Japanese media as usual lamented U.S. tactics of using sanctions threats in trade disputes, but saved their harshest words for the nation's costly domestic port practices and their own government's delay in tackling the problem.

"Criticism and dissatisfaction with this system from owners of goods and shipping companies have been smouldering," said an editorial in financial daily Nihon Keizai Shimbun. "But until recently, there has been no debate within Japan."

The paper said: "The influence of the JHTA, which in effect controls labour-management discussions, is immense and this issue has even been said to be taboo." Japanese harbours are often whispered to be controlled by "yakuza" gangsters.

"The government has said this is a private-sector matter for discussion between labour and management, closed its eyes to the dissatisfaction of users and stood idly by without improving the situation," the editorial said.

The mass-circulation Mainichi Shimbun also charged that Japanese officialdom had dragged its feet for too long over the issue and said there was some truth in U.S. complaints that Japan's port practices were too complex and costly.
"When we consider that the United States has repeated its demand for for quite some time, rather it is Japan's response which was too slow," the Mainichi said.
Japanese shipping companies, who will be hit hard if the sanctions go into effect, also say they are victims of the port practices set-up rather than its beneficiaries.

The two sides could meet as early as next week for talks to try to avert sanctions and settle the problem, but a Japanese government official said on Thursday it could take until the end of March for Tokyo to come up with a new proposal.
